This is Gule Wamkulu. 17th century.
on_screen: Title card: Gule Wamkulu · Malawi · 17th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Gule Wamkulu dates back to the great Chewa Empire of the seventeenth century.
Despite missionary bans and colonial pressures, the society survived by adopting Christian aspects, leading modern Chewa men to belong to both Christian churches and the Nyau society.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed at post-harvest seasons, weddings, funerals, memorial services, and chief installations or deaths, serving as a communication channel with ancestors and a vehicle for moral instruction.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform with intricate footwork, flinging dust into the air, responding to specific drumbeats and songs.
Zoomorphic structures involve turning around and around in a motion known as Nyau yolemba.
Watch for Nyau yolemba.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Masks and costumes are constructed of wood, straw, and feathers, categorized into feathered net masks, wooden face masks, and massive zoomorphic basketry structures called zilombo covering the entire body.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key characters include Kasinja (messenger/moderator), Chabwera kumanda (the grave returner), Simoni (colonial caricature), Maliya (kind-hearted female ancestor), Njobvu (elephant), and Kasiyamaliro (antelope).
Practiced across central and southern Malawi, eastern Zambia, western Mozambique, and among Chewa migrants in Zimbabwe (such as in Mabvuku and Highfield).
Rooted in the Nyau secret society cosmology and the 17th-century Chewa Empire, continuing centuries-old ancestral worship traditions.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Gule Wamkulu is a sacred secret-society ritual representing ancestral spirits; uninitiated individuals and outsiders are discouraged from approaching or are chased away, and identifying the men behind the masks is strictly forbidden.
